Kano State Governor, Abba Yusuf, has said no woman should lose her life because she cannot afford medical care, and no child should be denied treatment because of their family’s circumstances. The governor stated this during the launch of the launch of the Expanding Maternal and Child Health Insurance Scheme targeting 20,000 vulnerable women and children under five. Yusuf said the initiative, launched in partnership with the National Health Insurance Authority, was part of efforts to reduce maternal and infant deaths, improve access to healthcare and protect families from the financial burden of medical treatment. Speaking at the launch in Kano on Thursday, the governor said the scheme, tagged Mama Pikin – Whole Family Covered, will enrol the beneficiaries into the Basic Health Care Provision Fund through the Kano State Contributory Healthcare Management Agency over six months. The governor said beneficiaries would receive antenatal care, safe delivery, postnatal services and essential child healthcare at accredited primary healthcare facilities without payment at the point of service. “No woman should lose her life because she cannot afford medical care. No child should be denied treatment because of the circumstances of the family. And no household should be pushed into poverty by the cost of an illness,” he said. Yusuf said the state government was committed to reducing maternal and child mortality through investments in healthcare facilities, equipment and personnel. He disclosed that the state had renovated, rebuilt or upgraded more than 500 primary healthcare centres, while working towards ensuring that every ward had a functional health facility. We therefore respectfully request that, as this initiative delivers results, the Federal Government and NHIA consider Kano for its scale-up across all 44 Local Government Areas,” he said. The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof Ali Pate, said the scheme would strengthen access to essential healthcare and ensure that financial constraints did not prevent women from receiving medical attention. “Our vision for maternal health in Nigeria is clear: every woman should be able to seek care in time, receive the care she needs and bring her child safely into the world; without the cost of care standing between her and help,” Pate said. FG pledges to eliminate Noma, expand access to treatment Kano distributes 484 tricycle ambulances to boost rural healthcare Bauchi targets 1.5 million children for vitamin A supplementation He disclosed that the Federal Government had disbursed N249.6bn to the Basic Health Care Provision Fund nationwide over the past three years, while its Emergency Obstetric and Newborn Care programme was operating in more than 270 hospitals across the country. Pate said the new initiative would prioritise vulnerable women of reproductive age and children, while extending coverage to eligible members of their households. He, however, stressed that enrolment alone would not guarantee improved healthcare outcomes unless beneficiaries could access quality services when needed. “Families must be able to use their coverage when they need care. Women must know where to go. Facilities must be ready to provide appropriate services. And when a woman needs emergency care, the system must respond,” he added. The Director-General of the NHIA, Dr Kelechi Ohiri, said the programme would prioritise vulnerable women of reproductive age and children, with coverage extended to eligible members of their households. He said the Kano State Contributory Healthcare Management Agency would lead implementation by identifying beneficiaries, monitoring their use of services and ensuring they understood how to access care. The Executive Secretary of the agency, Dr Rahila Aliyu Muktar, said the scheme was designed to address financial barriers that often prevent women from seeking timely medical attention. “Out-of-pocket payment remains the greatest barrier between our mothers and the care they need. Too often, a family must choose between a hospital bill and food on the table, and too often, delay costs a life,” she said. Muktar said the agency had increased enrolment under the Basic Health Care Provision Fund from 108,664 beneficiaries in 2023 to more than 300,000. She added that more than 600,000 enrollees accessed healthcare services across 611 facilities in 2025, while the agency would monitor the new initiative and report its progress monthly. She said the agency would monitor the new initiative and report its progress monthly, stressing that its success would be measured by improved health outcomes rather than the number of insurance cards issued. “Our success will not be measured by the number of cards issued, but by the number of mothers who deliver safely, the children who grow up healthy, and the families spared from financial hardship,” she said.
